extracted.intended_audience: machine learning researchers, conference authors, program chairs, and reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation criteria for making machine learning conference papers reproducible, including code/data sharing, reporting of experimental details, and use of a reproducibility checklist. Targeted at authors, reviewers, and conference organizers implementing reproducibility programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproducibility: obtaining similar results as presented in a paper or talk, using the same code and data (when available). (Distinguished from Replicable, Robust, Generalisable — see Figure 1.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report focuses primarily on this notion of Reproducibility (re-doing an experiment using the same data and same analytical tools). It notes related concepts: Replicable (different data), Robust (same data, different analysis or reimplementation), and Generalisable (different data and different analysis but same conclusions). Specify which notion the work aims for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code and Data Availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Make code and data publicly available and easily accessible (long-term); provide links or repositories and ideally a DOI for code/data used to produce the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NeurIPS policy: authors may submit supplementary material (up to 100MB) and 'highly encourage' code submission. Expect (but not require) accompanying code for accepted papers that present experiments with a new algorithm; code need not be mandatory at initial submission but is expected by camera-ready. When data are confidential, provide complementary results on an open benchmark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear description of mathematical setting / algorithm / model
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a clear description of the mathematical setting, algorithm, and/or model used in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is question in the ML reproducibility checklist (authors answered this for 97% of submissions). It is considered baseline: manuscripts are expected to contain such a description; ambiguity here indicates under-specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of how experiments were run
rubrics_metrics.description: For all figures and tables that present empirical results, include a description of how the experiments were run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklist item during NeurIPS: authors should indicate experimental protocol details (e.g., training loop, data pre-processing steps, exact commands). This includes what was run, in what order, and any orchestration scripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report train / validation / test splits
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly document the dataset splits used (training, validation, test) and how they were created.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklist and discussion emphasize items related to test/validation/train splits. If nonstandard splitting or cross-validation is used, provide precise procedures and seeds or scripts to reproduce splits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report hyper-parameter ranges and tuning procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Document hyper-parameter ranges, the search procedure, and which hyper-parameters were chosen for reported results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under-specification of hyper-parameters is a frequent cause of irreproducibility; checklist items specifically ask for hyper-parameter ranges. Include search ranges, optimization strategy (grid, random, Bayesian), number of trials, and selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear definition of measures and statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a clear definition of the specific measure or statistics used to report results (what is being measured and how).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklist item highlighted that 87% of papers agreed this was important; authors should define metrics precisely (e.g., micro vs macro, top-k, exact computations) and any pre-/post-processing used to compute them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report central tendency and variation (mean & variation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe results with central tendency (e.g., mean) and variation (e.g., standard deviation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should report multiple runs' summaries (mean/std) rather than single-run numbers. The checklist asked for central tendency & variation and many submissions omitted variation even when metrics were defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly defined error bars / uncertainty quantification
rubrics_metrics.description: Include clearly defined error bars for reported results when applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The checklist explicitly asks for error bars; if used, state whether they represent standard error, standard deviation, confidence intervals, etc., and how they were computed (number of runs, bootstrap, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper statistical analysis and tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appropriate statistical methods to analyze results and support significance claims; avoid improper use of statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper warns against claiming significance without proper statistical testing or using the wrong statistical test. Provide justification for tests used and ensure assumptions are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple trials / random-seed reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Run sufficient independent trials (e.g., different random initializations) and report their results to capture variability due to randomness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites work showing methods can vary with different random initializations; authors should report number of seeds, seed values or seed-generation process, and per-run results or aggregated statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selective reporting and adaptive overfitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not selectively report only favorable results or tune on test data; document all relevant experiments and negative results where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selective reporting and adaptive overfitting are named causes of irreproducibility. Authors should disclose the full experimental regime and how hyper-parameters were chosen to avoid cherry-picking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions matched to evidence (avoid over-claiming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not draw conclusions that go beyond the evidence provided by the experiments and analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report flags 'over-claiming' as a common problem; ensure claims are proportionate to empirical support and acknowledge limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient number of experiments to support claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct and report a sufficient number of experiments to support the paper's claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insufficient number of experiments is listed as a reproducibility failure mode; provide sample sizes, number of runs, and experiment replications as appropriate for the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document computational infrastructure and resource requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify compute requirements, hardware, and software environment used (e.g., GPU type, number, wall-clock time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges that some experiments require impractical compute; documenting infrastructure helps assess feasibility and reproduce results or approximate them. Use containerization/environment capture when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle data confidentiality and proprietary software responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: When datasets or software cannot be released (privacy/IP reasons), provide mitigations such as complementary open-benchmark results or detailed preprocessing scripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy discussion notes legitimate reasons for non-release. Recommended practices: run complementary experiments on public datasets, provide detailed descriptions and synthetic or partial data when possible, and state limitations explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make artifacts discoverable and archived (long-term accessibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure code, data, and other artifacts are discoverable and preserved (e.g., repository with DOI) for long-term access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice for final submissions is to deposit artifacts in repositories and cite them; ephemeral links are discouraged. Long-term accessibility increases transparency and community uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reproducibility tooling / packaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tools that encapsulate environments and experiments (e.g., Docker, ReproZip, WholeTale) to aid reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report recommends but does not mandate specific tooling. Such tools can package OS, dependencies, code, experimental variables, and data to enable re-running experiments more reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage independent reimplementation (robustness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize value in independent reimplementations: availability of original code is helpful but reimplementation tests robustness and can reveal mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Availability of code helps verification but is not a guarantee of correctness; encourage both sharing original artifacts and community reimplementations to assess robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt minimal reporting checklists
rubrics_metrics.description: Use reporting checklists to require minimal information in manuscripts (e.g., dataset splits, hyper-parameter ranges, experimental setup).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NeurIPS ML reproducibility checklist (v1.2) was used at submission and camera-ready. Checklists are intended to improve completeness of reporting; reviewers may find them useful in assessing soundness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artifact evaluation and badging
rubrics_metrics.description: Use artifact evaluation mechanisms (e.g., badges) to indicate when papers meet standards for artifact availability, reproducibility, and replication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report references ACM badges and artifact review as mechanisms to signal trustworthiness. Conferences/journals may adopt badge systems or artifact-evaluation tracks to incentivize reproducible practices.
